lead: An aircraft flies on electricity as much as on fuel: generators, batteries and converters feed every instrument, light and control on board. This unit follows the power from the generator to the busbar, through protection and conversion, into the instruments the pilot reads. After it you can trace a supply path, size a protection device, read an airspeed or EGT indicator, and explain why the A320 and the B787 are wired so differently.
about: The unit starts at the source: how a generator's output is regulated, switched onto a busbar and protected (3.1), then how converters change it into the forms each load needs (3.2). Batteries (3.3) and emergency sources (3.4) keep the aircraft alive when generators drop out. It then goes to the parts that use and carry power: lighting (3.5), avionics packaging, cooling and EMI (3.6), air data and engine instruments (3.7, 3.8), voltage regulators (3.9), wires and circuit protection (3.10), bus configurations and switching (3.11), and two real architectures, the A320 and the B787 (3.12). It closes with engine and fuel quantity indication (3.13).

chapters.idea: Every electrical load on the aircraft is fed from a generator whose voltage is held steady, whose output is switched onto a busbar, and whose faults are removed by protection before the wiring is damaged.
chapters.depth: DC generation with shunt and compound DC generators; AC generation at 115 V 400 Hz from an integrated drive generator (IDG, constant speed) and variable-frequency generation at 360-800 Hz; 28 V DC and 270 V DC systems. Typical DC system chain: generator, voltage regulator, reverse-current cut-out, busbar, loads. Typical AC system chain: generator, generator control unit (GCU, also called generator control and protection unit), generator circuit breaker (GCB), AC bus, transformer rectifier unit (TRU). Protection functions at block level: over-voltage, under-voltage, over-current, over-excitation, under-frequency and over-frequency, differential or earth (ground) fault, generator drive disconnect. Know what each protects and what trips it. Keep the internal circuits out.

figure.title: One generator channel, from shaft to load
figure.aria: A generator feeds a contactor and busbar while the control unit senses voltage and commands both the field and the contactor to trip.

chapters.example: A twin-engine aircraft has two 28 V DC generators rated 200 A each. Non-essential loads draw 180 A and essential loads draw 60 A. One generator fails. (a) How much load must be shed? (b) What is the load on the surviving generator once all non-essential loads are dropped? Answer: total load is 240 A, one generator gives 200 A, so 40 A must be shed; after shedding all non-essential loads the survivor carries 60 A, well inside its 200 A rating.
chapters.trap: Assuming the failed generator's contactor opens for every fault, and confusing 400 Hz constant frequency from an IDG with the 360-800 Hz of a variable-frequency system.
chapters.prereq: First-year DC and AC circuit theory: Ohm's law, three-phase power, power factor.
chapters.leave: TRUs, inverters and auto-transformers to 3.2; battery charging and cell behaviour to 3.3; RAT and PMG to 3.4; busbar arrangements to 3.11; wire and breaker selection to 3.10.

chapters.idea: Converters change the form of electrical power (AC to DC, DC to AC, or AC at a lower voltage) so that each load receives exactly the voltage and frequency it was designed for.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter in detail. Inverter: DC to AC, static (SCR or transistor bridge) replacing the older rotary inverter, output 115 V 400 Hz single or three phase for AC instruments and synchros. Transformer rectifier unit (TRU): three-phase transformer plus full-wave bridge, 115 V AC to 28 V DC, typical ratings of 100-200 A, feeding DC buses and charging the battery; efficiency and heat load matter. Auto-transformer: one winding with tapped sections, steps 115 V down to 26 V for instrument lighting and synchro reference; it gives no isolation. Current transformer for load sensing and its burden. Depth: block diagram, waveforms in words, rating and efficiency calculations, no semiconductor device physics.

figure.title: Conversion between the AC and DC buses
figure.aria: The AC bus feeds a transformer rectifier unit that makes 28 V DC, and the DC bus feeds an inverter that remakes 115 V AC for the standby bus, with the battery able to drive the inverter when generators are lost.

chapters.example: A TRU is rated 200 A at 28 V DC and is 92 % efficient. It is fed from a 115 V three-phase AC bus at unity power factor. Find the DC output power, the AC input power and the line current drawn. Answer: output = 28 x 200 = 5600 W; input = 5600 / 0.92 = 6090 W; line current = 6090 / (1.732 x 115) = 30.6 A.
chapters.trap: Treating an auto-transformer as an isolation transformer, and forgetting efficiency when working out the AC input current of a TRU.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for where the AC and DC buses come from.
chapters.leave: Rectifier and transistor circuit detail to the electronics course; battery charging behaviour to 3.3; PMG and backup converters to 3.4.

chapters.idea: The battery is the only source of power with the engines off, and it carries the essential loads for the short time between losing all generators and getting another source online.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the chemistry and testing detail; the comparison is standard. Lead-acid: 12 cells at about 2.1 V each giving a 24 V battery, sulphuric acid electrolyte, specific gravity near 1.28 used as a state-of-charge check, strong cranking current, heavy per ampere-hour. Nickel-cadmium: 19 or 20 cells at about 1.25 V each, potassium hydroxide electrolyte, sintered plates, low internal resistance, good cold performance, long life, but prone to thermal runaway and voltage depression; cell count differs from lead-acid for the same nominal voltage. Common ground: ampere-hour capacity and the C-rate, capacity check discharge, constant-current then constant-voltage charging, temperature sensing, deep discharge damage. Some syllabi also list lithium; give it one short paragraph on higher energy per kilogram and the fire risk that follows.

figure.title: Terminal voltage against capacity discharged, at the 1-hour rate
figure.aria: The nickel-cadmium curve stays almost flat until about ninety percent discharge and then falls sharply, while the lead-acid voltage falls steadily from the start.

chapters.example: A 24 V lead-acid battery rated 40 Ah at the 1-hour rate supplies 40 A for 30 minutes. (a) How many ampere-hours are used? (b) What is the depth of discharge? (c) If the load then drops to 20 A, how long will the remaining charge last? Answer: (a) 40 x 0.5 = 20 Ah; (b) 20/40 = 50 %; (c) the remaining 20 Ah at 20 A lasts 1 hour, ignoring rate effects.
chapters.trap: Assuming a 24 V nickel-cadmium battery has the same 12 cells as a lead-acid one, and taking a specific-gravity reading straight after topping up the electrolyte.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 and 3.2, because the battery sits on the DC bus and is charged through a TRU or a dedicated charger.
chapters.leave: Charger circuits to 3.2; battery installation, venting and servicing procedures to the maintenance course.

chapters.idea: When every main generator is lost, a small air-driven generator or a permanent magnet generator keeps the essential instruments, radios and controls alive long enough to reach an alternate.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this at depth. Ram air turbine (RAT): a small propeller pushed into the airstream, driving a generator of a few kVA and often a hydraulic pump; automatic and manual deployment, an airspeed band in which it may be deployed, and its place on the emergency AC bus feeding an essential TRU. Permanent magnet generator (PMG): a magnet rotor with a fixed stator winding mounted on the engine or APU, used for ignition and control power, with no field winding so it cannot be switched off electrically; output frequency rises with shaft speed. Backup converters: battery to essential DC bus, static inverter to AC standby bus. ETOPS: Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards, the 60, 120 and 180 minute diversion rules for twins; explain only the electrical consequence, which is how long one generator plus APU start and battery must carry the aircraft.

figure.title: Emergency supply chain after generator loss
figure.aria: Loss of all generators deploys the ram air turbine, whose small generator feeds the emergency AC bus and an essential transformer rectifier, while the battery and the permanent magnet generator hold up the essential DC bus in the meantime.

chapters.example: An aircraft is cleared for ETOPS 120, so it must stay within 120 minutes of a suitable alternate; at 420 kt that is 840 nm. Its essential DC bus draws 2.8 kW at 28 V. The battery is rated 40 Ah and only 50 % may be used. Find the bus current and the time the battery can carry it, and say what this means for the diversion. Answer: 2800/28 = 100 A; usable charge = 20 Ah; time = 20/100 h = 0.2 h = 12 min, so the RAT or the APU must take over long before 120 minutes.
chapters.trap: Believing the battery can cover the full ETOPS diversion time, and forgetting the RAT has an airspeed band outside which its output is unusable.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the main sources and 3.3 for battery capacity and usable charge.
chapters.leave: APU starting, ignition and the hydraulic side of the RAT to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Aircraft lights are grouped by who they serve (crew, cabin, outside world), and each group gets its own supply, control and failure requirement.
chapters.depth: Internal: flight compartment flood, integral instrument panel, chart and dome lights, standby lighting; cabin ceiling, sidewall, reading and galley lights, controlled from the cabin panel (some syllabi show this control panel on an A300 simulator); emergency egress lighting, exit signs and floor-proximity lights on their own battery packs. External: navigation or position lights (red on the left, green on the right, white at the tail), anti-collision beacons and strobes, landing and taxi lights, logo and wing or engine scan lights. Supplies: 28 V DC and 115 V AC 400 Hz for some fittings; dimming by rheostat or pulse-width control; why emergency lights sit on the essential bus. Depth: purpose, position, supply and control of each group, plus simple load and endurance sums.

figure.aria: The lighting tree splits into internal groups for the cockpit and cabin and external groups for navigation, anti-collision and landing lights, with emergency egress lighting picked out.

chapters.example: A cabin emergency lighting pack is rated 24 V, 4 Ah with a maximum current of 6 A. It must run 12 exit-sign lamps at 6 W each and 20 floor-proximity lights at 3 W each for 12 minutes. Will it hold? Answer: total power = 72 + 60 = 132 W; current = 132/24 = 5.5 A, inside the 6 A limit; energy used = 5.5 x 0.2 h = 1.1 Ah, which is 27.5 % of the 4 Ah rating, so yes.
chapters.trap: Putting emergency egress lights on a normal AC bus instead of a dedicated pack, and swapping the red and green navigation lights.
chapters.leave: Display brightness, annunciator philosophy and cockpit human factors to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An avionics box must survive heat, vibration and electrical interference, so standards fix its mechanical form, its cooling path and the interference limits it must meet.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Packaging: line replaceable unit (LRU), rack and front-loading trays, hold-down clamps and connectors; ARINC 404 and ARINC 600 case and connector standards, and DOD (military) types with their harsher environmental standards; weight, volume and access for replacement on the ramp. Cooling: natural convection, forced air through the avionics bay, cold-plate mounting, liquid loops on newer types; the thermal resistance path from junction to cooling air and its limits. EMI/EMC: conducted and radiated emission and susceptibility, shielding, screened twisted pairs, grounding and bonding, filter connectors, separation of power and signal routes; the environmental and interference standards by name only (DO-160, MIL-STD-461). Depth: block-level cause and cure, one thermal calculation.

figure.title: Layers that control interference, from the source outward
figure.aria: Five stacked layers control interference, starting with suppression inside the box and ending with bonding to the airframe.

chapters.example: An LRU dissipates 120 W. Its cold plate has a thermal resistance of 0.15 K/W to the cooling air, and the inlet air is at 30 degrees C. (a) Find the case temperature. (b) The airflow is halved and the resistance doubles; the case limit is 70 degrees C. Is there still margin? Answer: (a) 30 + 120 x 0.15 = 48 degrees C; (b) 30 + 120 x 0.30 = 66 degrees C, so only 4 degrees C of margin remains.
chapters.trap: Assuming a box that passes on the bench will pass in the bay with reduced airflow, and mixing up conducted emission with radiated emission.
chapters.prereq: First-year heat transfer (thermal resistance) is enough; no earlier chapter is required.
chapters.leave: ARINC 429, MIL-STD-1553B and AFDX data buses, and IMA rack architecture, to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The airspeed indicator and the altimeter both measure pressure and convert it into a number the pilot can act on: airspeed from the difference between total and static pressure, altitude from static pressure alone.
chapters.depth: Pitot-static system: pitot (total) pressure P0, static pressure P, impact pressure q = P0 - P. Airspeed indicator: capsule and linkage, the calibration at sea-level ISA density, the relation q = 1/2 rho V squared, indicated, calibrated and true airspeed, the coloured arcs (white flap range, green normal, yellow caution, red radial for Vne). Altimeter: aneroid capsule and static port, the subscale (Kollsman) knob and QNH setting, pressure altitude against true altitude, the ISA lapse rate, roughly 27 ft per hPa near sea level. Error sources for both: position error, leak, lag, temperature error, blockage with pitot heat as the cure. Depth: principle, construction, calibration and one calculation each.

figure.title: Pitot-static feeds to the three pressure instruments
figure.aria: The pitot port feeds only the airspeed capsule, while the static port feeds the airspeed capsule, the altimeter capsule and the vertical speed indicator.

chapters.example: (a) At sea level, where air density is 1.225 kg/m3, an aircraft has an impact pressure of 2500 Pa. Find the indicated airspeed in m/s and in knots. (b) The altimeter subscale is set to 1013.25 hPa and the static pressure outside is 950 hPa. Find the pressure altitude. Answer: (a) V = square root of (2 x 2500 / 1.225) = 63.9 m/s, and 63.9 x 1.944 = 124 kt; (b) 1013.25 - 950 = 63.25 hPa, and 63.25 x 27 = about 1710 ft.
chapters.trap: Mixing up which port feeds which capsule, reading indicated airspeed as true airspeed, and forgetting that the altimeter only reads height above the set pressure level.
chapters.prereq: Basic pressure and density ideas from physics; no earlier chapter is needed.
chapters.leave: Air data computers and how the values travel on a data bus to Unit 4; the use of these values in navigation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Engine instruments report how fast and how hot the engine is running, and each one turns a mechanical quantity into an electrical signal at the sensor.
chapters.depth: Tachometer: mechanical drive shaft, DC tacho-generator (a small generator whose voltage rises with speed), magnetic or variable-reluctance pickup counting teeth, and frequency measurement where pulses per second = (rpm/60) x teeth; N1 (fan or LP) and N2 (core or HP) read as percentage of a reference speed. Exhaust gas temperature: thermocouple with a hot junction in the exhaust and a cold junction at the indicator or in a compensating circuit, type K (chromel-alumel) sensitivity about 41 microvolt per degree C, cold junction compensation, amplifier, moving-coil or digital display, start and take-off limits. Mention cylinder head temperature and the turbine gas temperature name used on some engines. Depth: signal chain and one calculation per instrument.

figure.title: Two sensor chains reaching one cockpit display
figure.aria: A shaft-driven tacho generator sends a speed signal and an exhaust thermocouple sends a millivolt signal through an amplifier, both ending at the cockpit indicator.

chapters.example: (a) A magnetic pickup faces a gear with 30 teeth on the HP shaft. The indicator reads 9000 rpm. Find the pulse frequency. (b) A type K thermocouple with a sensitivity of 41 microvolt per degree C has its hot junction at 700 degrees C and its cold junction at 25 degrees C. The amplifier gain is 100. Find the voltage reaching the converter. Answer: (a) 9000/60 = 150 rev/s, so 150 x 30 = 4500 pulses per second; (b) 41 x (700 - 25) = 27 675 microvolt = 27.7 mV, and 27.7 x 100 = 2.77 V.
chapters.trap: Using the hot junction temperature alone instead of the difference between hot and cold junctions, and confusing N1 percent with N2 percent.
chapters.prereq: Basic electrical measurement; no earlier chapter is required.
chapters.leave: Sensor construction, signal conditioning and ADC detail to Unit 4; FADEC and engine control to Unit 1; fuel and ignition systems to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A generator's voltage rises with speed and falls with load unless its field current is controlled, so a regulator compares the output with a reference and adjusts field current to hold voltage constant.
chapters.depth: Principle: generated emf depends on field flux and speed, so control the field. Vibrating-contact regulator: a solenoid and spring open and close a contact that inserts resistance in the field circuit, the duty cycle setting the average field current, about plus or minus 1.5 % regulation, with contact wear and radio noise. Carbon-pile regulator: a stack of carbon discs whose resistance falls as pressure rises, a solenoid varies the pressure, smooth and contactless but slow and temperature sensitive. Electronic regulator: Zener reference, error amplifier, transistor or thyristor, or pulse-width control of the field, plus over-voltage and under-voltage cut-out, over-excitation limiting and reverse-current protection, giving better than plus or minus 0.5 %. Compare the three on accuracy, speed, wear and noise.

figure.title: Closed loop voltage regulation
figure.aria: The output voltage is sensed, compared with a Zener reference, and the error drives the field winding in a closed loop that corrects the output.

chapters.example: A 28 V DC generator has a field resistance of 10 ohm and the regulator inserts a 20 ohm series resistance when its contact opens. The average field current needed is 1.5 A. (a) Find the duty cycle. (b) With no load the output is 28.4 V and at full load 27.6 V; find the regulation. Answer: (a) contact closed gives 28/10 = 2.8 A, open gives 28/30 = 0.93 A; 2.8 D + 0.93 (1 - D) = 1.5 gives D = 0.57/1.87 = 0.305, so 30.5 %; (b) (28.4 - 27.6)/27.6 x 100 = 2.9 %.
chapters.trap: Thinking the regulator adds resistance in the load line instead of the field circuit, and forgetting that the vibrating contact works by duty cycle, not by a fixed resistance.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the generator, its field and the GCU.
chapters.leave: Generator construction and load sharing to 3.11; the protection relays that sit beside the regulator to 3.1.

chapters.idea: Every wire can carry a stated current and survive a fault current for a stated time, so the protection device is chosen from the wire's derated rating, not from the load alone.
chapters.depth: Wire and cable: stranded copper, silver or nickel plated for high temperature, insulation of PVC, PTFE, Kapton or glass braid, gauge in AWG, current rating and derating for bundle size, altitude and ambient temperature, voltage drop limit of a few percent, marking, clamping and bend radius. Circuit protection: fuse (one-shot, inverse time-current curve), current limiter (a heavy-current, fast-acting fuse for feeder protection), limiting resistor (in series to hold fault or inrush current down; some syllabi list it under protectors), circuit breaker (thermal bimetallic, magnetic, thermal-magnetic, trip-free so it cannot be held closed on a fault, remote-controlled types), and why breakers are preferred in flight since they can be reset. Coordination: the device curve must lie below the wire damage curve and above the normal load current.

figure.title: Breaker trip curve against the wire damage curve
figure.aria: The breaker curve sits below the wire damage curve at every current, so the breaker trips before the wire is overheated.

chapters.example: A 28 V DC feeder carries 40 A for 6 m from the bus to a load. The conductor is 8 AWG copper with a resistance of 0.63 milliohm per metre, and the return path doubles the length. (a) Find the voltage drop as a percentage of 28 V. (b) Find the power lost in the cable. (c) Suggest a breaker rating. Answer: (a) length = 12 m, R = 0.63 x 12 = 7.56 milliohm, drop = 40 x 0.00756 = 0.30 V, which is 1.1 %; (b) 40 squared x 0.00756 = 12.1 W; (c) a 50 A breaker, provided the derated wire rating is at least 50 A.
chapters.trap: Choosing a fuse from the load current alone and ignoring the wire's derated rating, and resetting a tripped thermal breaker again and again instead of finding the fault.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the busbar and feeder arrangement.
chapters.leave: Busbar layouts and bus tie logic to 3.11; generator feeder protection settings to 3.1.

chapters.idea: How generators are joined to the busbars decides whether one fault takes out half the aircraft or one bus, and switches and relays are the devices that make and break those joins.
chapters.depth: Busbar as a copper or aluminium bar feeding a group of loads. Split bus: each generator feeds its own bus with no paralleling, simple and fault-contained, but a generator loss leaves its bus on the battery or the opposite TRU. Parallel bus: generators run together on one bus, needing synchronising checks, equal load sharing by voltage droop or a load controller, and frequency control. Split-parallel: normally split, tied through bus tie breakers after a failure so one generator can carry both buses. Single-engine and twin-engine layouts, DC and AC versions. Switches: toggle, push-button, rotary selector, microswitch and proximity switch. Relays and contactors: coil and contacts, normally open and normally closed, latching, contact rating, the suppression diode across a DC coil, and solid-state power controllers. Control versus protection.

figure.aria: Two generators feed their own buses through generator contactors, a bus tie breaker can join the two buses, and the essential bus has feeders from both plus a battery standby path.

chapters.example: Two 28 V DC generators run in parallel on a 300 A load. Each has a no-load voltage of 28.5 V. Generator 1 drops 0.4 V per 100 A and generator 2 drops 0.6 V per 100 A. Find the current shared by each and the bus voltage. Answer: the terminal voltages are equal, so 28.5 - 0.004 I1 = 28.5 - 0.006 I2, giving I1 = 1.5 I2; with I1 + I2 = 300, I2 = 120 A and I1 = 180 A; bus voltage = 28.5 - 0.004 x 180 = 27.78 V.
chapters.trap: Believing parallel generators must be set to exactly equal voltages, when they share by droop, and assuming AC generators can be paralleled without a synchronism check.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for generation and protection and 3.9 for the regulator that sets each generator's voltage.
chapters.leave: Relay and solid-state device construction to Unit 4; contactor protection settings to 3.1.

chapters.idea: The A320 and the B787 mark the two ends of the design range: the A320 keeps a conventional 115 V AC 400 Hz and 28 V DC mix, while the B787 moves most loads to 235 V AC variable frequency and 270 V DC.
chapters.depth: A320: two engine-driven integrated drive generators of 90 kVA at 115 V 400 Hz, an APU generator of similar size, an emergency generator driven by the ram air turbine, transformer rectifier units feeding 28 V DC buses, and nickel-cadmium batteries; generators are controlled by GCUs and joined through generator and bus tie contactors. B787: a bleedless, more-electric architecture with large starter-generators on each engine producing 235 V AC variable frequency (about 360-800 Hz), transformer rectifier units making 270 V DC, APU starter-generators, and lithium-ion batteries; because frequency varies with engine speed, every load must accept it and no constant-speed drive is fitted. Compare on voltage level, frequency, sources, conversion and cable weight. Why higher voltage pays: for the same power, current falls as voltage rises.

figure.title: The B787 more-electric supply chain
figure.aria: Engine and APU starter-generators feed a 235 V AC variable-frequency bus, transformer rectifier units make 270 V DC, and both feed the essential buses with the ram air turbine as the final backup.

chapters.example: A 100 kW three-phase load at unity power factor is supplied first at 115 V and then at 235 V. Find the line current in each case and the ratio of cable copper loss. Answer: at 115 V, I = 100 000 / (1.732 x 115) = 502 A; at 235 V, I = 100 000 / (1.732 x 235) = 246 A; loss goes as current squared, so the ratio is (502/246) squared = 4.2, meaning the higher voltage cuts the loss by about four times for the same cable.
chapters.trap: Assuming the B787's variable-frequency output needs a constant-speed drive, and forgetting that a variable-frequency bus forces every connected load to tolerate the frequency range.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for generation and protection, 3.2 for conversion and 3.11 for bus arrangements.
chapters.leave: Engine starting and bleed air architecture to Unit 2; display and data bus architecture to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Beyond speed and temperature the cockpit needs pressure, flow and fuel remaining, and fuel quantity is the hardest of these because it is measured inside a tank that moves and changes temperature.
chapters.depth: Engine indicators: oil pressure and fuel pressure from a Bourdon tube or a pressure transducer, fuel flow from a turbine or paddlewheel meter, torque for turboprops, vibration from an accelerometer, all grouped on the engine display; primary indicators (N1, EGT, and on some types N2) against secondary indicators; starting indicators such as starter valve and ignition lights. Fuel quantity: float and rheostat on light aircraft; capacitance gauging on transports, where the fuel between the probe plates replaces air and raises capacitance, and C = epsilon A / d; tank units, a compensator unit that corrects for the fuel's dielectric constant, indication in kilograms using density, the refuelling panel, and drip sticks as a check. Errors from aircraft attitude, temperature and fuel type; fuel flow integration as a cross-check.

figure.title: Capacitance fuel quantity measurement
figure.aria: Fuel rising between the probe plates raises capacitance, the bridge and compensator convert it, and the result is shown in kilograms and checked against integrated fuel flow.

chapters.example: A capacitive fuel probe has plates of area 0.02 m2 separated by 5 mm. The dielectric constant is 1.0 for air and about 2.0 for fuel, and the permittivity of free space is 8.854 x 10^-12 F/m. Find the capacitance when the tank is empty, half full and full, taking the fuel level as the filled height between the plates. Answer: empty C = 8.854e-12 x 0.02 / 0.005 = 35.4 pF; full C = 2 x 35.4 = 70.8 pF; half full C = 35.4 + (70.8 - 35.4)/2 = 53.1 pF.
chapters.trap: Assuming capacitance follows tank volume in an irregular tank, and forgetting that the fuel's dielectric constant shifts with temperature and fuel type, which is what the compensator exists to fix.
chapters.prereq: 3.8 for the engine indicator chain; basic capacitance from first-year physics.
chapters.leave: Display formats and EICAS or ECAM presentation to Unit 4; fuel plumbing, refuelling and tank layout to Unit 2.
